lessons.title: How a Company's Life Stage Shapes Its Funding Options

children.text: Two founders walk into the same bank branch in Pune on the same morning, both asking for ₹2 crore. The first runs a 15-year-old machine shop with ₹40 crore of revenue, steady profits and a factory in its own name. The second has a six-month-old logistics app, no revenue, four laptops and a very good pitch deck. The bank will happily discuss a loan with the first and will politely decline the second. Neither answer is unfair. They are the same answer to two very different businesses.
Where a company sits in its life determines who is willing to fund it, on what terms, and how much it will cost. Get this wrong and you waste months pitching to the wrong people.

body.text: Lenders fund certainty. Equity funds uncertainty. As a company's cash flows become more predictable, its funding options widen and its cost of money falls.

children.text: The Funding Staircase
Indian companies typically climb through five stages. Each stage unlocks sources that were closed at the one before.

body.caption: Who funds a company at each stage

cells: 1. Idea and pre-seed
No product, no revenue, one to three people
Founders' savings, friends and family, incubators, government grants
Own capital, grants, small equity cheques
2. Early startup
Product live, early customers, still loss-making
Angel investors, angel networks, seed funds
Equity shares, CCPS, convertible notes
3. Growth
Revenue growing fast, still burning cash
VC and PE funds, venture debt funds, some NBFCs
Preference shares, venture debt, working capital limits
4. Mature private company or SME
Profitable, predictable, owns assets
Banks, NBFCs, PE funds
Term loans, cash credit, PE investment
5. Listed or large corporate
Scale, track record, public disclosure, a credit rating
Public shareholders, institutions, bond investors, banks
IPO, QIP, rights issue, NCDs, commercial paper, ECB

body.text: Notice the direction of travel. At stage 1 almost the only money available is equity, and it is the most expensive money a company will ever take. By stage 5 the company can choose from a wide menu and borrow at single-digit rates. Surviving long enough to climb the staircase is itself worth a great deal.

children.text: Why the Bank Said No to the App
Lenders and equity investors are not evaluating the same thing. A lender is asking whether it will get its money back. An equity investor is asking how large this could become.

columns.label: A bank lending money asks
points: Do you have three years of audited financials and profits?
Is there predictable cash flow to service the EMI?
What is your credit history and your rating?
Are promoters willing to give a personal guarantee?
What is the downside if the business merely survives?

columns.label: A VC or angel investing asks
points: How large can this market get?
Can this team execute faster than others?
Is growth accelerating, even if losses are too?
What could this be worth in seven to ten years?
Who else is on the cap table?
What is the upside if the business wins big?

children.text: This is why a pre-revenue startup with no
collateral

cannot borrow, no matter how promising it is. A bank that is repaid its 10% interest does not benefit at all if the startup becomes a unicorn, so it cannot afford the failures. An equity investor whose one big winner returns 50 times can afford nine failures out of ten.

markDefs.definition: An asset a borrower pledges to a lender, which the lender can sell to recover its money if the borrower does not repay. Also called security.

body.title: Whose money is this?
body.question: A two-year-old Bengaluru biotech startup has no revenue, no patents granted yet, rented lab space and needs ₹5 crore to run clinical trials over three years. Which source is realistic?
options: A bank term loan against the lab equipment
An equity round from a specialist venture fund, possibly alongside a government grant
A cash credit facility from an NBFC
body.explanation: No revenue, no collateral of any value and a three-year wait for any outcome. Nothing about this can be serviced with fixed monthly payments, so debt is out. Deep-tech and biotech at this stage are funded by specialist equity investors and by grants, which do not need to be repaid at all.

children.text: Stage 1 and 2: The Indian Early-Stage Menu
Founders often assume the only options are savings or a venture fund. India has a wider early-stage menu than that, including government schemes designed precisely because banks will not lend here.

body.caption: Government-backed support for early-stage and small Indian businesses

cells: Startup India Seed Fund Scheme
Up to ₹20 lakh as a grant for proof of concept, prototype or product trials, and up to ₹50 lakh for market entry and scaling through convertible debentures or debt-linked instruments
Applied for through DPIIT-approved incubators, not directly. Total scheme outlay of ₹945 crore
Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana
Collateral-free loans for micro enterprises: Shishu up to ₹50,000, Kishore up to ₹5 lakh, Tarun up to ₹10 lakh and Tarun Plus up to ₹20 lakh
For income-generating micro businesses, not for tech startups. Tarun Plus is for borrowers who have repaid a Tarun loan
CGTMSE credit guarantee
A government-backed guarantee that lets banks lend to micro and small enterprises without collateral, with guarantee cover raised to ₹5 crore from 1 April 2023
The business still has to qualify on cash flows. The guarantee replaces security, not creditworthiness

body.label: Startup India Seed Fund Scheme
body.description: The official portal. Browse the list of approved incubators, check eligibility conditions and see what each incubator funds before applying.

body.text: Grants and guarantee schemes look like free money and are not. Grants come with milestones, reporting and usage conditions. A CGTMSE-backed loan is still a loan: the guarantee protects the bank if you default, not you.

children.text: Stage 2 and 3: What Equity Costs You
Early-stage equity is priced in ownership, not interest. If a startup agrees a
pre-money valuation
of ₹8 crore and raises ₹2 crore, the post-money valuation is ₹10 crore and the new investor owns a fifth of the company.

markDefs.definition: What a company is agreed to be worth immediately before new money comes in. Add the amount raised to get the post-money valuation.

body.caption: The share of the company handed over in a funding round

body.title: How much did they give away?
body.prompt: A Jaipur D2C brand raises ₹2 crore at a pre-money valuation of ₹8 crore. What percentage of the company do the new investors now own?
body.explanation: Post-money valuation is ₹8 crore plus ₹2 crore, which is ₹10 crore. The investors own ₹2 crore of ₹10 crore, which is 20%. The founders now own 80% of a company that the round says is worth ₹10 crore, instead of 100% of one worth ₹8 crore.

body.title: Why founders should care about the order of rounds, not just this one

children.text: Each round dilutes everyone who came before it. A founder who gives away 20% at seed, 20% at Series A and 18% at Series B does not have 42% left. Ownership multiplies rather than subtracts.

Starting at 100%, after the three rounds above the founders hold 0.80 x 0.80 x 0.82, which is about 52%. Add an ESOP pool and the figure drops further. This is why the amount raised at an early stage matters so much: money taken when the valuation is lowest costs the most ownership.
Cap table mechanics are covered properly in the dedicated cap table courses on this platform. For now, hold on to the principle: raise as much as you genuinely need and no more, especially early.
Stage 3: The In-Between Instrument
Between "no bank will touch you" and "banks compete for you" sits
venture debt
. Indian funds such as Alteria Capital, Trifecta Capital and Stride Ventures lend to startups that have already raised institutional equity.

markDefs.definition: Loans made to venture-backed startups that banks will not lend to, usually alongside or just after an equity round, at higher interest and often with warrants attached.

body.label: What venture debt typically looks like in India
body.value: Interest in the mid-teens, plus warrants, on a 2 to 3 year tenor
body.context: Priced well above a bank loan because the borrower is loss-making, and well below equity in terms of ownership given away. Usually sized as a fraction of the equity round it follows, and used to extend runway or fund working capital without another round of dilution. Terms vary widely by deal, so treat these as indicative.

body.text: Venture debt is not a substitute for equity. It is borrowed against the cash an equity round has already put in the bank. If a startup cannot raise its next equity round, venture debt repayments become the first thing that breaks.

children.text: Stage 4 and 5: The Menu Opens Up
Once a company is profitable and predictable, its funding problem changes completely. It is no longer asking whether anyone will fund it. It is choosing which source is cheapest.
Bank term loans and working capital limits
: the default for profitable SMEs and large corporates alike.
Private equity
: large cheques for established businesses, often buying out an existing shareholder.
IPO
: the first sale of shares to the public, listing on NSE and BSE.
[[Qualified institutional placement]]
: for companies already listed, a fast way to sell new shares to institutions.
Non-convertible debentures
: borrowing from bond investors instead of a bank, usually needing a credit rating.
Commercial paper

: very short-term borrowing of 7 days to 1 year, in denominations of ₹5 lakh, open only to companies with a net worth of at least ₹4 crore and a sanctioned working capital limit, under the RBI's 2024 directions.
[[External commercial borrowings]]
: raising loans from lenders outside India, within RBI limits.

body.title: Indicative annual cost of money by stage (%)

body.text: These figures are illustrative, not quotes. Equity has no stated rate at all: the number shown is the annual return investors hope to earn, which is what makes it expensive for the company. Actual rates depend on the borrower, the rating, the security offered and where interest rates are at the time.

children.text: One Company, Ten Years
Gati Robotics is a fictional Coimbatore company building warehouse automation. Its funding history shows the staircase in one picture.

body.title: The funding journey of a company that makes it

events.title: Founders and a grant
events.description: Two engineers put in ₹25 lakh of savings and win a ₹20 lakh proof-of-concept grant through a DPIIT-approved incubator. No outside ownership given up beyond the founders themselves.

events.title: Angel round
events.description: ₹2 crore from an angel network at a ₹8 crore pre-money valuation, for 20% of the company. Used to build the first commercial product.

events.title: Series A
events.description: ₹25 crore from a venture fund, structured as compulsorily convertible preference shares. Revenue is ₹6 crore and losses are widening on purpose.

events.title: Venture debt and first bank limits
events.description: ₹8 crore of venture debt to extend runway, plus a small working capital limit from a bank now that receivables from large customers exist.

events.title: Profitable, so the bank returns
events.description: A ₹40 crore term loan at single-digit interest funds a new plant, secured against the plant itself. No dilution at all.

events.title: IPO
events.description: A ₹600 crore issue lists the company on NSE and BSE. Early investors sell part of their stake through an offer for sale, and the fresh issue funds expansion.

stats.label: Year 7 money
stats.context: Cheapest capital of its life so far

body.title: The one-line rule
body.explanation: A lender's upside is capped at its interest rate, so it needs to be confident of repayment. An equity investor shares in unlimited upside, so it can accept that many investments will fail.

body.title: Pick the cheapest workable source
body.question: A profitable 20-year-old auto components maker in Chennai, with a factory in its own name and ₹120 crore of revenue, needs ₹15 crore to buy a new machine that will be in use within six months. Which is the most sensible first option?
options: A private equity investor buying 15% of the company
A secured bank term loan against the new machine and the factory
body.explanation: The company has profits, collateral and a track record, which is exactly what a lender wants. A term loan is by far the cheapest source here and costs the owners no ownership. Selling 15% of a profitable 20-year-old business to fund one machine would be an extremely expensive way to buy it.

body.title: Advising two founders in the same week
body.scenario: You work in an HR and L&D role at a business incubator in Kochi that supports early-stage companies. Two founders in your cohort ask for guidance. Priya runs a 14-month-old B2B software company with ₹40 lakh of annual revenue, growing fast, losing money, no assets beyond laptops. Rahul runs a five-year-old profitable packaging unit with ₹9 crore of revenue, a small factory in his own name and steady orders from two FMCG customers. Both need about ₹1.5 crore.
body.prompt: What funding routes would you point each of them towards, and what would you warn each about?
body.modelAnswer:
Priya sits at stage 2. No collateral, no profits and a fast-growing but unproven model means a plain bank loan is very unlikely. Realistic routes: an angel round or a seed fund, a Startup India Seed Fund Scheme application through a DPIIT-approved incubator if she qualifies, and possibly a convertible note if she wants to postpone setting a valuation. Warn her that ₹1.5 crore raised at a low early valuation is expensive in ownership, that she should raise against a specific 12 to 18 month milestone rather than a round number, and that grant money comes with milestones and reporting.

Rahul sits at stage 4. Profitable, asset-owning and predictable, which is exactly what lenders want. Realistic routes: a secured bank term loan against the factory or the new equipment, an NBFC if he needs speed over price, and CGTMSE-backed lending if collateral is the sticking point. Warn him that selling equity here would be the most expensive option available to him, that he should compare the all-in cost across at least three lenders rather than accepting his existing bank's first offer, and that a loan sized to his worst recent quarter is safer than one sized to his best.

The common lesson for your cohort: the right answer is set by the stage of the business, not by which instrument sounds more impressive.

body.title: Work out which stage your company is actually in
steps: Does the business have audited financials for the last three years?
Has it been profitable in at least two of those years?
Does it own assets that could serve as collateral?
Are its monthly cash inflows predictable enough to cover a fixed EMI in a bad month?
Does it have a credit rating, or could it get one?
Is it listed, or large enough to consider listing?
If you answered no to most of these, you are in equity territory. If yes to most, debt is almost certainly cheaper.

cards.definition: Idea stage. Funded by founders, friends and family, incubators and grants.
First outside equity, usually a few crore, from individuals or angel networks.
Loans to venture-backed startups, mid-teens interest plus warrants, alongside an equity round.
Government-backed guarantee enabling collateral-free bank lending to micro and small enterprises, cover up to ₹5 crore.
Collateral-free micro enterprise loans: Shishu, Kishore, Tarun and Tarun Plus, up to ₹20 lakh.
Qualified institutional placement. A fast share sale by a listed company to institutional investors.
Short-term unsecured borrowing, 7 days to 1 year, ₹5 lakh denominations, for companies with a net worth of at least ₹4 crore.
External commercial borrowings. Loans raised from lenders outside India within RBI limits.

points: A company's life stage, not its ambition, decides which funding sources are actually open to it.
Lenders need predictable cash flows and collateral, which early-stage companies do not have.
Equity is the only real option at the idea and early stages, and it is the most expensive money a company will ever take.
India has government-backed routes for the stages banks avoid: the Startup India Seed Fund Scheme, Mudra loans and CGTMSE guarantees.
Venture debt sits between the two worlds and is borrowed against equity already raised, not against profits.
By the time a company is profitable and listed, it can pick from a wide menu and borrow in single digits. Certainty is what made the difference.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Gati Robotics and the other unnamed businesses are fictional illustrations. Scheme limits and eligibility conditions change, so verify current terms on the official portals before acting. Cost ranges shown are indicative and not quotes.
